demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I have permanently changed for the worse

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with the more trauma-disconnected pattern implied by emotionless/numb recall and sensory reliving. Those can occasionally coexist, but this combination is clinically questionable as a compact 3-item profile because one item suggests relatively integrated verbal access while the others suggest poorly integrated or detached trauma memory.

issues.item: Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
issues.explanation: 'Door and Lock Checking' is a poor fit for the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. It implies an intruder/home-security threat that is not supported by the other selected Memory or Negative Appraisal items, which center more on guilt, identity change, and trauma recall rather than fear of break-in or assault. This makes the Threat profile less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, repeated checking of doors and windows being locked suggests a home-intrusion/interpersonal danger theme that is not supported by the other threat, memory, or appraisal items. The rest of the profile centers on guilt, altered self-view, disconnection, and poorly elaborated trauma memory rather than fear of external attack.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Loss of connection to community and culture is not impossible, but in this profile it is insufficiently linked to the stated trauma and the other selected items. The other appraisals focus on self-doubt and identity change after causing harm, whereas this item introduces a broader sociocultural rupture that is not reflected elsewhere in memory or threat content, making the node less coherent.

vignette: Leila, a 31-year-old social media manager of Lebanese descent, remembers the day as if the air had thickened. She was in a warehouse loading a shipment of new camera lenses for a high-profile client when a stack of metal boxes toppled. In the chaos, her elbow brushed the shoulder of Omar, a coworker who was setting up a camera rig. The impact was sudden and painful; Omar's hand went limp, and she felt the weight of his shock as a sudden, visceral sting. Leila's mind froze; she was still gripping the box when she heard Omar's ragged breath, the sharp metallic clink of a bent steel support, and the acrid scent of burnt plastic from a nearby power supply. She knows the taste of that metal, and she can still smell the faint, oily perfume of the machinery that day. The memory of the incident is fragmented-she cannot find the right words to describe how the world tilted-but the smell lingers, a cruel reminder of the moment she thinks of the sound of his collapsed body. The weight of her self-criticism grew instantly after the accident. Leila had always prided herself on her careful, methodical work, but now she was haunted by doubts that her judgment had failed, that she could never be the safe, reliable person she had wanted to be. These feelings of self-doubt, she began to interpret as proof that she could not control her environment, that danger was an ever-present threat. The fear of being wrong made her hyper-vigilant; a sudden brush of a hand at the office, a casual wave, set her heart racing, and she reacted with alarm even when nothing was threatening. The self-doubt also pulled her back into the memory of the warehouse, turning a once one-off accident into a persistent narrative that replayed each time she felt uncertainty. Leila's attempts to revisit the warehouse scene were not aimed at closure but at understanding the why of her lingering distress. The more she forced the memory into her mind, the sharper the scent of metal became, and the more the memory seemed to justify her growing sense of self-doubt. Each recall reinforced the belief that she was unrecognizable to herself now-her former calm, confident self had been replaced by a stranger who could not trust her own actions. The memory, in turn, amplified her sensitivity to touch; she started to see every unintended contact as a potential echo of that fateful collision, and the startle response she exhibited in the office was no longer a fleeting moment but a constant state of alertness. When a colleague, Lina, casually nudged her sleeve to get her attention over a project deadline, Leila's body reacted before her mind could assess the situation. The sudden contact triggered a rush of adrenaline, and in the brief instant she recalled the warehouse's metallic scent and the sharp pain of Omar's collapse. The flash of memory intensified her fear, reinforcing the belief that she could never be safe or reliable. That same fear loop fed her negative appraisals-she felt she had irrevocably changed, that she was permanently damaged, and that every touch was a potential reminder of failure. The loop of threat and memory made her withdraw from spontaneous physical interactions at work, and she began to avoid any situation that might provoke a sudden contact. The cumulative effect of these cycles manifested in Leila's work life and relationships. She found herself refusing to meet clients in person, canceling phone calls, and spending long hours editing posts that discussed accident safety, hoping to distract herself. Her relationships with friends frayed as she stayed home from gatherings to avoid any chance of being touched or startled. Over months, these avoidance habits eroded her sense of self, leaving her feeling isolated and unrecognizable. It was this sense of loss that pushed her to seek therapy. The day she finally decided to see a therapist, she was overwhelmed by the fear of confronting the memory she could no longer find words for, yet she was also desperate for relief from the constant, unspoken threat that kept her on edge. Leila hopes therapy will help her untangle the relentless cycle of self-doubt, startle, and memory so that she might once again feel safe in her own body and regain the sense of self she lost in the warehouse that day.
